CILIA AND FLAGELLA The cilia (L. cili = eye-lash) and flagella (L. flagellum = little whip) are microscopic, contractile and hair-like or thread-like motile structures that originate inside the cell from the basal bodies but are present outside the cell. They aid in movement, locomotion, feeding, and circulation. Englemann (1868) first reported the presence of flagellum. Occurrence Cilia are present in all protozoans of the class ciliate, flame cells of flat worms, in some larval forms e.g. Bipinnaria larva of starfish, in some body structures e.g. wind pipe, fallopian tubes, etc., ciliated epithelium of the metazoa, etc. Flagella are found in all the protozoans of the class flagellate, choanocyte cells of sponges, gastrodermal cells of coelenterates, spermatozoa of metazoa and lower plants, zoospores of algae, gamete cells, etc.

Ultrastructure Both flagella and cilia have similar structures: basal body, rootlets, basal plate, and shaft. In fact, term cilium is used when it is shorter than a cell (5 - 20 μm), while the longer extension is called flagellum (100 - 200 μm). A cross-section of either organelle reveals a pair of central filaments surrounded by nine peripheral filaments, forming a 9 + 2 arrangement. This bundle of filaments is known as an axoneme or axial filament. It is encased in a double-layered protective coat, 90 angstroms thick, which is continuous with the plasma membrane. Each peripheral microtubule is a doublet, consisting of two subtubules, 'A' and 'B'. The 'A' microtubule has pairs of dynein arms, which can hydrolyze ATP. The central filaments are connected to the 'A' microtubules of the peripheral Biology, Grade 11 | 53
filaments by radial spokes. The movement of cilia and flagella is powered by ATP, which diffuses from the cell cytoplasm.

Chemically, the central tubules are made of dynein protein, while the peripheral microtubules are made of tubulin protein. Dynein acts as an ATPase enzyme, breaking down ATP to release energy for the beating of cilia and flagella.

1. Cilia or flagella bring locomotion in organisms by their power strokes and return strokes.
2. Cilia of Paramecium and flagella of collar cells of sponges set up current in water allowing nutrition-and respiratory gas enter inside the body.

3. Ciliary movements in the respiratory tract help to eliminate solid wastes out of the body. 4. Cilia in kidney-nephrons cause movement of nephric filtrate. 5. Cilia push eggs out of the oviduct in amphibians and mammals. 6. Cilia help larval forms to disperse. 14. NUCLEUS Nucleus (L., nucleus = kernel) is a double membrane bound protoplasmic body comprising genetic information which regulates all the cellular activities and carries the hereditary information of the cell. It is the largest cell organelle embedded in the cytoplasm. It was first discovered by Robert Brown (1833) in plant cells.

A true nucleus (Eukaryon) is found in all the eukaryotes except mature mammalian RBCs, sieve tube cells of phloem, tracheids and vessels of xylem. The prokaryotes have an incipient nucleus called nucleoid or prokaryon or genophore (the nucleus without nuclear membrane and nucleolus). Its shape and size varies. Generally, its shape depends upon the shape of the cell. However, it could be spherical, cuboidal, ellipsoidal, discoidal or even irregular. Its size depends upon nueleo-cytoplasmic index and the number of chromosomes present in the nucleus. In young cell, nucleus occupies 25% of cell volume while in mature cell, it occupies about 10% of cell volume.
